interface.name: agora_shell

description.summary: the window server's own window management

interface.description:
One global. It hands out the three objects above it: a window, which is what a surface becomes, an output, which is where the work area comes from, and a window list, which is what a shell component asks for.
**THE VERSION IS THE CAP ITS CHILDREN INHERIT, WHICH IS WHY IT MOVED AND ITS OWN REQUESTS DID NOT.** Wayland hands a new object the version of the object that made it, so an `agora_window` can only reach version 3 through a shell bound at 4. Version 2 added no request HERE; it is `agora_window.set_reserved` that arrived, and a shell bound at 1 keeps handing out version 1 windows. **VERSION 3 ADDED** `get_window_list`, `activate_window` and `close_window`, and **VERSION 4 ADDED NOTHING HERE**: it carried `agora_window.set_activatable`, the door a Dock needs and no application does. **VERSION 5 ADDED `reopen_window`**, the question a tile asks when the application has nothing to raise. **VERSION 6 ADDS `get_dock_menu` and `dock_menu_action`**: the two halves of a tile's menu, and the first thing in this protocol that carries a MENU rather than a window's property. **VERSION 7 ADDS THE SELECTION**: `set_selection`, `clear_selection`, `request_selection` and the five events that carry an offer, an fd, or a refusal — the first thing in this protocol that says anything about an application other than the one being talked to. See `CLIPBOARD-PLAN.md` for why the compositor owns it, why the transfer is an fd rather than a copy, and what a client bound below 7 never sees. **VERSION 8 ADDS `agora_window.set_badge` AND `agora_window_list.badge`**: the short label an application's Dock tile shows, PUSHED by the application and carried on the snapshot the Dock already takes — a badge changes when the application decides, and a Dock that asked each tile each refresh would spend a round trip to learn "nothing". The badge is its own event rather than another argument on `window`, because an older list must not be handed a wire it cannot parse. **VERSION 9 ADDS FRACTIONAL SCALE**: `agora_output.preferred_scale` and `agora_window.set_buffer_scale_fixed`, the pair that lets an application rasterise at the display's real dots per inch instead of at an integer multiple the compositor then resamples. A point is 1/72 inch; an integer `wl_output.scale` cannot say 1.333, so the client hears the fraction here and the compositor places its buffer 1:1. **VERSION 10 ADDS `agora_window.set_sheet_parent`**: the one statement this protocol has ever carried about TWO windows of the same client, and the reason it has to be a statement rather than an inference — see that request for why the pair cannot be read off the frames. **VERSION 11 ADDS `agora_window.set_cursor`**: the pointer's SHAPE, which until now was the compositor's alone. A window says which of its theme's cursors the pointer should be while it is over that window, and the compositor applies it when the window under the pointer changes — see that request for why the shape belongs to the window and not to the seat.

enum.name: error

description.summary: what this global can refuse

enum.description: A surface has ONE role, and the two role protocols disagree about who decides the size — so a surface that already has one is refused rather than quietly obeying two contradictory models.

entry.name: already_has_role
entry.summary: that surface already has a role

request.name: get_window

description.summary: give a surface the role of a window

request.description: A surface with no role is never composited, so this is what makes a surface a window. It is the counterpart of `xdg_wm_base.get_xdg_surface` and may not be combined with it on the same surface: a surface has ONE role, and the two roles disagree about who decides the size.

request.name: get_output

description.summary: ask an output for its work area

request.description: `wl_output` describes what a screen IS — its geometry and its mode. This describes what is LEFT of it, which is a question only the window server can answer because the answer depends on the furniture the server owns.

request.name: get_window_list

description.summary: ask to be told what windows this server has

request.description:
**THE DOCK'S DATA SOURCE, AND THE ONE QUESTION AN APPLICATION NEVER ASKS.** An ordinary client knows its own windows and has no business knowing anyone else's. A shell component is the opposite: its job is to show what is running, and it cannot learn that from its own process. So a client that asks gets an `agora_window_list`, which the server fills with a snapshot now and again whenever the set changes.
**IT IS ASKED FOR RATHER THAN GIVEN**, because the snapshot is re-sent on every change — every title, every map and unmap, every focus change — and an application that never asks must not pay for a Dock's bookkeeping. The list is created on the first request and lives until the client goes away.

request.name: activate_window

description.summary: bring a window forward and give it the keyboard

request.description:
**THE ONE THING A CLICK ON A DOCK TILE IS.** `raise` moves a window within its level and does not touch the focus, because on the Mac the focus is the user's click together with `-makeKeyAndOrderFront:`. A click on a Dock tile is a click — just not on the window — so this is that pair, said by the component the click landed on: the window is raised in its level AND takes the keyboard, which is what its application's menu bar follows.
**ID IS FROM THE WINDOW LIST**, and it is the list's number because the asking client holds no proxy for somebody else's window and cannot get one: a window object belongs to the client that made it. An id nothing answers is ignored rather than an error — a Dock racing a window that just closed is ordinary, and a protocol error there would kill the Dock.
**NO PERMISSION MODEL, SAID OUT LOUD.** Any client may activate any window, as any client may read the list. Agora's split is the Mac's — shell components are trusted with the desktop — and a real check belongs with the session that launches them, not with every request here.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: a window id from the window list

request.name: close_window

description.summary: ask a window's application to close it

request.description: **THE OTHER HALF OF A DOCK TILE'S MENU, AND THE EVENT `agora_window.close` FINALLY HAS A SENDER.** The event was declared from the first version and nothing ever sent it — which is what "the event is the server's to send when the session ends" looks like when there is no session. A Dock's Quit is the same request by a different route: the application is ASKED, exactly as it is asked by its own close button, because the decision to close is the application's (`-windowShouldClose:` and everything behind it). A client that ignores the event stays open, which is the Mac's behaviour and the reason Force Quit is a session concern rather than a protocol one.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: a window id from the window list

request.name: reopen_window

description.summary: ask an application to show a window again

request.description:
**WHAT A CLICK ON A TILE MEANS WHEN THE APPLICATION HAS NOTHING TO RAISE.** A click is `activate_window` for every window the application has — and an application can be running with no window a person can work in, because the desktop a shell draws is furniture at a level below every window. On the Mac that click still does something: the application is asked to reopen and IT decides what that means (Finder opens a window). This is that question.
**THE WINDOW IS THE ADDRESS AND NOT THE SUBJECT.** Both sides name each other by window id and nothing else, so the asking client names any window of the application — the frontmost one is the honest choice — and the server forwards `agora_window.reopen` to that window's client. The window itself is not opened, closed, raised or focused by this; what "again" means is the application's answer, not the server's. An id nothing answers is ignored, exactly as `activate_window`'s is.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: any window of the application, from the window list

request.name: get_dock_menu

description.summary: ask an application for the menu its tile should offer

request.description:
**A DOCK'S RIGHT-CLICK, ASKED OF THE APPLICATION IT LANDED ON.** `window` is any window of that application from the window list — the frontmost one is the honest choice — and it is an ADDRESS rather than a subject, exactly as `reopen_window`'s is: the answer is the application's, and the server forwards `agora_window.dock_menu_requested` to the window's client and nothing else.
**THE ANSWER ARRIVES ON THE `agora_dock_menu` THIS ASKED FOR**, and it is that object that makes the round trip possible: a window id names a window, and the server needs to know WHICH CLIENT asked in order to hand the answer back. The client destroys the object once it has the answer, has given up waiting, or has gone away.
**AN ASK THE SERVER CANNOT FORWARD IS ANSWERED EMPTY, IMMEDIATELY.** The window may be gone, may belong to an `xdg_toplevel` with no `agora_window` at all, or may be an `agora_window` bound below version 6 — and in every one of those cases the honest answer is "this application has no dock menu", said now rather than left for a timeout to say later. A shell component is a client of a protocol that grows, and it must not hang because it asked an older one.
**SEVERAL ASKS MAY BE OUTSTANDING, AND EACH IS ANSWERED.** A person can right-click two tiles, or the same tile twice; every pending `agora_dock_menu` naming that window hears the answer, because the answer is the application's and not the ask's.

arg.name: window
arg.summary: any window of the application, from the window list

request.name: dock_menu_action

description.summary: the person chose an item of the application's dock menu

request.description:
**THE OTHER DIRECTION, AND THE REASON THE MENU'S CONTENTS HAVE TO CROSS AT ALL.** The Dock draws the menu — it is the Dock's panel, at the Dock's screen edge, with the Dock's own items under the application's — so the item the person picked is not the application's object and cannot send the application's action. What the Dock knows is the ID the application gave that item in the description it published, and this sends it home: the server forwards `agora_window.dock_menu_action` to the window named here, and the application finds its own item and performs it. The AppKit does that on both sides (`NSDockMenu`), and the ids are its to number.
An id nothing answers is ignored, exactly as `activate_window`'s stale id is: a menu dismissed as its application quits is ordinary.

arg.name: window
arg.summary: the window the menu was asked about

arg.name: item
arg.summary: the id the application gave the item it published

enum.name: selection_refusal

description.summary: why a selection request could not be served

enum.description: **THREE ANSWERS, BECAUSE THEY MEAN THREE DIFFERENT THINGS TO A READER** — and because silence, which is what a protocol without them would give, cannot be told apart from "there is nothing on the clipboard". A paste that silently becomes the empty string is the failure people actually hate.

entry.name: wrong_type
entry.summary: an owner exists but cannot serve that type

entry.name: owner_gone
entry.summary: the owner disappeared between the offer and the request

request.name: set_selection

description.summary: this client owns the selection, and these are the types it can serve

request.description:
**IT REPLACES WHATEVER WAS THERE, FROM WHICHEVER CLIENT, AND THERE IS NO FOCUS CHECK.** A background application may own the selection — that is what "copy from a window that just lost focus" means — and gating this on focus would be a policy nobody asked for.
The types are MIME types (`text/plain;charset=utf-8`, `image/png`), in the owner's order of preference, and **THE ARRAY IS THEIR BYTES RATHER THAN AN ARRAY OF POINTERS**: an `array` is opaque to Wayland, so the strings are written back to back with a NUL after each. A client that marshals a `char **` sends pointers to itself, which is a mistake the server now cannot make on its behalf. The server announces them to every client as `selection_offer`, one event per type, preceded by `selection_lost` if there was a previous owner — so a reader has exactly one transition to handle.
**NOTHING IS SENT WITH THIS REQUEST.** The owner produces bytes only when somebody asks (`selection_requested`), which is what keeps the server out of the data path entirely.

arg.name: types
arg.summary: MIME types this client can serve, each NUL-terminated, back to back

request.name: clear_selection

description.summary: this client no longer owns anything

request.description: The owner giving the selection up while it is still running. Every client hears `selection_lost`. An owner that destroys its shell resource — or whose connection goes away — has the same effect without asking.

request.name: request_selection

description.summary: give me a readable fd for this type

request.description:
**THE ANSWER IS A FILE DESCRIPTOR, NOT DATA.** The server creates a pipe, hands the WRITE end to the owner (`selection_requested`) and the READ end to the asker (`selection_sent`). The owner writes and closes; the asker reads to EOF. Nothing passes through the server: no bytes, no size limit, and no way for a hostile owner to make the compositor allocate a payload.
A request that cannot be served is answered immediately and specifically with `selection_refused`, never by silence. A request that CAN be served is answered with the fd BEFORE the data is written — the promise is the fd, and EOF is the end of the payload. A reader that must not block reads with `O_NONBLOCK` and treats `EAGAIN` as "not yet".

arg.name: mime_type
arg.summary: the type wanted, exactly as it was offered

event.name: selection_offer

description.summary: the selection offers this type

event.description: One event per type, sent to every client when the selection changes, after any `selection_lost` that came with the change. **UNSOLICITED**, which is what makes the reader's cache possible: a client that wants to know what can be pasted knows it without asking, and a client that does not care ignores this.

event.name: selection_lost

description.summary: there is no selection any more

event.description: The owner cleared it, destroyed its resource, or was replaced. A reader's cache is empty from this moment.

event.name: selection_requested

description.summary: somebody wants this type; write it into fd

event.description: To the OWNER. The fd is the write end of a pipe whose read end is already on its way to the asker. The owner writes the bytes, closes the fd, and is done; the server neither knows nor cares how much was written.

arg.name: fd
arg.summary: write the payload here, then close it

event.name: selection_sent

description.summary: here is the fd the owner will write into

event.description: To the ASKER. The fd is readable; EOF is the end of the payload, and an empty payload is a legitimate answer (an owner may offer a type it produces nothing for). The owner has been asked already, so a reader that blocks waits only on the owner.

arg.name: fd
arg.summary: read the payload here, to EOF

event.name: selection_refused

description.summary: that request cannot be served, and here is why

event.description: The answer to a `request_selection` that produced no fd. The reason is what lets a reader tell "there is nothing on the clipboard" from "there is something, but not that" from "it went away while I was asking".

interface.name: agora_dock_menu

description.summary: one answer to one `get_dock_menu`

interface.description: **A THING THAT EXISTS FOR THE LENGTH OF ONE QUESTION.** A window id names a window; the answer has to find the client that asked, and this object IS that name — the client makes one per ask and destroys it when the answer has been read. It carries one event and nothing else, because there is nothing else to say.

event.name: menu

description.summary: the application's dock menu, or an empty answer

event.description:
**`menu` IS THE APPLICATION'S OWN FORMAT, AND THIS PROTOCOL DOES NOT READ IT.** It is a description of an `NSMenu` — the AppKit at both ends is the same library, so the two sides agree about it, and the window server carries the string without interpreting a byte of it. The point of the rule is the one the dock rule always makes: the server must not grow a special case for what a menu IS, and a compositor that parsed one would have an opinion about items.
AN EMPTY STRING MEANS "THIS APPLICATION HAS NO DOCK MENU", which is an answer and not a failure: an application that implements nothing is the ordinary case, and a Dock shows its own items alone.
`app_id` is the identifier the application's window declared, so the asking client can check that the answer is about the application it asked about (a relaunch makes a new application with the same name).

request.name: destroy

description.summary: the answer has been read, or is no longer wanted

request.description: Destroys the object. Nothing is left behind on the server side: an ask is not a resource the server keeps once its answer has gone out, and one that is abandoned before the answer arrives is abandoned, which is what a client's timeout already means.

interface.name: agora_window_list

description.summary: what windows the server has, as a snapshot

interface.description:
**A SNAPSHOT RATHER THAN A DELTA.** A delta is worth its sequence numbers and its retries when a stream is long-lived and narrow; a desktop has thirty windows and the set changes when a person does something. So every change sends the WHOLE LIST — `begin`, one `window` per window, `done` — and a client that misses one snapshot is corrected by the next, with no state machine to get wrong.
**AND IT IS A LIST OF WINDOWS, NOT OF APPLICATIONS.** The window server only knows what is on the glass; an application with no windows is invisible to it, and that is the honest answer this interface gives. What a shell derives from it — "these are the running applications" — is a reading of the windows it can see, and the day a session component knows better the answer moves there rather than being faked here.

event.name: begin

description.summary: a snapshot starts

event.description: Sent before every snapshot, INCLUDING the empty one — a client that cleared its model on `begin` and rebuilt it from the `window` events would otherwise keep a closed window's tile for ever.

event.name: window

description.summary: one window, in stacking order from back to front

event.description:
**`id` IS THE NUMBER `activate_window` AND `close_window` TAKE.** It is the server's, not a client's, and it is stable for as long as the window object is.
`app_id` is the bundle identifier the application declared (`set_app_id`), which is what a dock groups its tiles by. `level` is the integer the window sits at, so a dock can ignore menus and the bar without the server deciding for it what a "real" window is. `active` says this window has the keyboard, which is the only notion of "frontmost" this tree has.

event.name: badge

description.summary: the label an application set for its Dock tile

event.description:
**A SEPARATE EVENT RATHER THAN ANOTHER ARGUMENT ON `window`.** Appending an argument to an existing event is the one change a versioned protocol cannot absorb: a client bound at version 1 would parse the old opcode with the new wire and read the wrong bytes. So the badge travels beside the window it belongs to — `id` is that window's number from the `window` event immediately before it, and a list bound at version 1 is never sent this event at all. One badge event per window per snapshot, between `begin` and `done`.
An empty label is the ordinary "no badge", and it is what an application that never sets one reports.

description.summary: the snapshot is complete

interface.name: agora_output

description.summary: an output, and the part of it an application may use

interface.description: A COMPANION TO `wl_output`, not a replacement: that interface is the surface a client needs to draw and this one is the one it needs to place itself.

event.name: work_area

description.summary: the frame minus the menu bar and the Dock

event.description: Apple's `NSScreen.visibleFrame`, in the output's coordinates. Sent when the client binds and again whenever it changes — because the Mac's answer to "the work area changed" is that THE APPLICATION CONSTRAINS ITSELF (`constrainFrameRect:toScreen:`), so the server's job is to say what happened and not to move anybody's window.

event.name: menu_bar_area

description.summary: the part of the menu bar an application's own menus may use

event.description:
**THE ONE NUMBER ABOUT THE MENU BAR THAT AN APPLICATION CANNOT DERIVE, AND THE REASON THIS EVENT EXISTS.** The server owns the bar's STRIP and the SYSTEM MENU at its left. Everything to the right of that square is where an application's own menus go — AND THE APPLICATION DRAWS THEM, because they are its menus. This event says where they may begin and nothing else: what goes in the space, and how wide each title is, is the application's business.
A CLIENT CANNOT WORK THIS OUT FOR ITSELF. The System menu's width is the server's, and it is the sort of number that changes with the system's language, its input methods, or a decision made in `window-server` — so an application that guessed would put its first menu UNDER the System menu the first time that width changed, and nothing would tell it. The work area above cannot carry it either: that is a VERTICAL reserve, and the Mac's `-visibleFrame` starts at x = 0 because the bar spans the whole screen. Two different questions, two different events.
**AND THE COLOUR IS IN THIS EVENT BECAUSE IT IS A PROPERTY OF THE BAR THE SERVER OWNS.** An application's menus sit IN the bar, and menus drawn on a panel of their own colour are a visible SEAM across a surface that is meant to be one thing. The alternative — every client picking a colour that looks close — is how two greys come to differ by four counts and nobody can say which one is right.

arg.name: colour
arg.summary: the strip's colour, 0xRRGGBB

event.name: preferred_scale

description.summary: device pixels per logical point, as a fraction

event.description:
**THE REAL SCALE, RATHER THAN `wl_output.scale`'S CEILING.** A point is 1/72 inch, so a 57.97-dpi panel has 0.805 device pixels per point and a 96-dpi panel has 1.333 — neither of which `wl_output.scale`, an integer, can say. A client that reads this event renders its buffer at `round(points * scale)` device pixels and declares that fraction with `agora_window.set_buffer_scale_fixed`; the compositor then places those pixels 1:1, which is what makes a 23-point button 23/72 inch tall on every panel without being resampled.
`wl_output.scale` is still sent as the integer ceiling for clients that do not speak this event, and a client that ignores this one keeps working exactly as it did — a little soft on a fractional output, but correct. Sent when the output object is created and again if the scale changes.

interface.name: agora_window

description.summary: a window, placed and sized by its application

interface.description: **THE APPLICATION IS HONOURED.** Every set_ here is a DEMAND the server writes down and acts on, not a request it may refuse or adjust — which is the inversion of `xdg_toplevel` and the whole point of this protocol. The server's share of the Mac's model is the shadow, the work area, and knowing who is in front.

enum.name: edge

description.summary: which side of the output a reservation is made against

enum.description: THE SIDES ARE THE OUTPUT'S, not the window's, and that is the whole of what a reservation says: "`amount` pixels along this side are mine, so they are not in the work area." It is not a claim about where the window IS — `set_frame` already said that and this file never second-guesses it. A Dock at the bottom reserves the bottom; a panel on the left reserves the left; the two are the same request.

entry.name: top
entry.summary: the top edge, where the menu bar is

entry.name: bottom
entry.summary: the bottom edge, where the Dock usually is

request.name: set_frame

description.summary: where the window is and how big it is

request.description: `NSWindow.setFrame:display:`, position included. The server honours it exactly: it does not cascade, it does not tile, and it does not move a window the application did not move. Constraining a frame to a screen is the APPLICATION's — `constrainFrameRect:toScreen:`, against the work area above — and a server that did it for the application would be doing it without knowing what the application knows.

arg.name: x
arg.summary: left edge, in output coordinates

arg.name: y
arg.summary: top edge, in output coordinates

request.name: set_status_item

description.summary: make this window an item the SERVER places in the status area

request.description: **THE ONE PLACE THE FRAME RULE DOES NOT REACH, AND THE HEADER IS WHY.** `NSStatusItem` declares `length`, `title`, `image`, `menu`, `target`, `action`, `highlightMode` and `view` — AND NO POSITION OF ANY KIND. A position is what an application placing its own item would need and could not have: it does not know what else is in the status bar, so it cannot know where its own item goes. So THE APPLICATION SAYS HOW LONG ITS ITEM IS AND THE SERVER PACKS IT, from the right edge of the menu bar leftwards, in the order the items were made. `set_frame` will not move such a window afterwards, because a status item is in the menu bar by definition. The two sentinel lengths AppKit has (`NSVariableStatusItemLength`, `NSSquareStatusItemLength`) are its own business: it resolves them to a width before asking, since only it knows how wide its view wants to be.

arg.name: length
arg.summary: how wide the item is, in output coordinates

request.name: set_level

description.summary: where the window sits in the stack

request.description: `NSWindow.setLevel:`, an INTEGER and not a member of a fixed set — so a menu window, a status item and the Dock can be ordered against each other and against ordinary windows without this protocol having anticipated any of them. A window with no level set is at the server's normal level.

request.name: raise

description.summary: bring the window to the front of its level

request.description: `NSWindow.orderFront:`. The application asks and the server honours. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE IS FOCUS: on the Mac that is the user's click together with `makeKeyAndOrderFront:`, and this protocol has no opinion about it yet.

request.name: lower

description.summary: send the window to the back of its level

request.description: `NSWindow.orderBack:`.

request.name: set_title

description.summary: the window's name

request.description: Which the application draws itself, as it draws its whole frame; the server records it for its own use — the menu bar of the active application, the window menu — and for anything describing windows to a person.

request.name: set_app_id

description.summary: which application this window belongs to

request.description: The Mac's bundle identifier, near enough: what the menu bar is switched by when this window becomes the active one, and what a launcher or a task list groups by.

request.name: set_visible

description.summary: put this window on the screen, or take it off

request.description: **THE DOOR `xdg-shell` DOES NOT HAVE, AND A REAL APPLICATION NEEDS EVERY DAY.** An `xdg_toplevel` is mapped or destroyed, so a client that wants to hide a window must DESTROY it and build another to show it again — and a menu that closes and reopens would make and throw away a surface each time. `-orderOut:` is not an exotic door: it is what every menu, every sheet and every panel does when it goes away.

arg.name: visible
arg.summary: zero takes it off the screen; anything else puts it back

request.name: set_pointer_grab

description.summary: receive the pointer when it is over no surface at all

request.description:
**THE DOOR A POPUP NEEDS, AND THE ONE THING A MOUSE CLICK CANNOT OTHERWISE SAY.** A Wayland compositor sends pointer events to the surface UNDER the pointer and to nobody when the pointer is over the desktop — so a menu could not hear the click that lands outside it, and "click anywhere to dismiss" was not expressible. While this is set, events that would go to NO surface are delivered to THIS one instead, with coordinates relative to it (which may fall outside its frame — that is how the client learns a click was outside).
IT IS A FALLBACK AND NOT A REAL GRAB, ON PURPOSE: a surface under the pointer still receives the event. A menu bar is the reason — the bar is a SEPARATE window from the menu it opened and the pointer must be able to cross back to it to switch menus, so routing EVERY event to the menu would break the one gesture a menu bar is for. `zero` releases it; destroying the surface releases it too.

arg.name: grab
arg.summary: nonzero takes it; zero gives it back

request.name: set_pointer_capture

description.summary: receive the pointer WHEREVER it is, until the button comes up

request.description:
**THE DOOR A DRAG NEEDS, AND THE OTHER HALF OF `set_pointer_grab`.** A window being resized or moved goes out from under the hand: the edge follows the pointer, the compositor's copy of the surface is a frame behind, and the pointer ends up over the DESKTOP or over ANOTHER WINDOW — where the events would go to somebody who is not dragging anything. MEASURED: a window resized out over a neighbour stopped following the pointer the moment the hand crossed onto it, and every motion after that went to the neighbour.
While this is set, pointer motion and pointer buttons are delivered to THIS surface and to nobody else, whatever is under the pointer, with coordinates relative to it (which may fall outside its frame). It is a REAL grab, which is exactly why it is a separate request from `set_pointer_grab`: that one must stay a fallback or a menu bar could not be crossed back to.
THE SERVER GIVES IT BACK ON ITS OWN when the last pointer button comes up — a capture is only ever meaningful mid-press — so a client that loses the release does not keep the desktop's pointer. `zero` releases it early, and destroying the surface releases it too.

arg.name: capture
arg.summary: nonzero takes it; zero gives it back

request.name: destroy

description.summary: the window is gone

request.description: Destroys the object. The surface outlives it and may be given another role, as it may under `xdg-shell`. **AND A RESERVATION GOES WITH IT**, because the reservation is this object's and the object is gone; see `set_reserved`.

event.name: close

description.summary: the server is asking the application to close

event.description: NOT the close button — that button is the application's, like the rest of the frame, and it is the application that decides what closing means. This is for the cases the server does know about: the session is ending, or a window manager's own affordance was used.

event.name: work_area_changed

description.summary: the work area this window is on has changed

event.description: The menu bar grew, the Dock moved, a screen went away. THE SERVER DOES NOT MOVE THE WINDOW: the application constrains itself, and this event is what tells it there is something to constrain.

event.name: pointer_global

description.summary: where the pointer really is, in OUTPUT coordinates

event.description:
**THE ONE COORDINATE A CLIENT-SIDE DRAG CANNOT DERIVE FOR ITSELF, AND THE REASON A FAST ONE WENT WRONG.** The title bar is the application's, so the drag is the application's too — but `wl_pointer.motion` reports the pointer RELATIVE TO THIS WINDOW, and a window that is being MOVED makes that a moving target: a hand that outruns the window puts the pointer on the desktop, the relative number chases its own tail, and the corrections COMPOUND. MEASURED: a fast drag moved the window zero pixels before the pointer grab, and hundreds of pixels past the pointer after it.
This is the ABSOLUTE position the relative one was computed from, sent immediately BEFORE it, so a client holding a grabbed point under the pointer can do it with one subtraction that does not depend on where the window happens to be. It is sent with button events too, because a drag's grab point is a button press.

arg.name: x
arg.summary: left, in output coordinates

arg.name: y
arg.summary: top, in output coordinates

request.name: set_reserved

description.summary: reserve a strip of the output for this window

request.description:
**THE WORK AREA IS THE SERVER'S TO SAY, AND THIS IS HOW A CLIENT CONTRIBUTES TO IT.** `NSScreen`'s `visibleFrame` is the frame minus the furniture, and on the Mac the furniture that is not the server's own is a WINDOW — the Dock's, which the window server sees and subtracts. Agora has no private CGS to derive that from, so the owner SAYS: `amount` pixels along `edge` are reserved, and every client's work area shrinks by it from that moment on.
**IT IS A REQUEST ABOUT THE SCREEN AND NOT ABOUT THIS WINDOW'S FRAME.** Nothing here moves the window, and `set_frame` is unaffected: a Dock may reserve 96 pixels at the bottom and then put its surface anywhere it likes. The two are separate answers to separate questions, and folding them together would be the server guessing what a level means.
**IT IS PER WINDOW BECAUSE ITS LIFETIME IS.** The reservation is released when the object is destroyed or when the surface goes away, so a Dock that crashes does not leave the desktop with a phantom strip missing. `amount` 0 releases it explicitly, which is what an autohiding Dock says before it hides — the Mac's answer to the same question: an autohidden Dock is not in `visibleFrame`.
**A WINDOW HAS ONE RESERVATION, SO ASKING AGAIN MOVES IT.** A second `set_reserved` replaces the first rather than adding to it, which is the Dock being dragged from the bottom to the side: one window, one strip, and no accumulated nonsense from where it used to be. Two edges at once is two windows — which is also what two panels are.
**AND SEVERAL WINDOWS MAY RESERVE THE SAME EDGE; THOSE AMOUNTS ADD.** That is the one aggregation that needs no owner to arbitrate: two panels on the left stop where each says the other begins, and no client is told which of the others is which. A server that took the maximum instead would hide the second one under the first and call it agreement.

arg.name: amount
arg.summary: pixels along that edge; 0 releases the reservation

request.name: set_activatable

description.summary: whether clicking this window may give its application the keyboard

request.description:
**THE DOCK'S SECOND REAL REQUEST, AND THE ONE THAT KEEPS THE MENU BAR WHERE IT WAS.** A click on a window gives that window's application the keyboard — `-makeKeyAndOrderFront:` and the user's click together — and the application's menu bar follows. That is right for every window a person works IN, and wrong for the furniture a person works THROUGH: clicking a Dock tile must activate the APPLICATION THE TILE NAMES, not the Dock, and a Dock that took the keyboard would take the menu bar with it and leave the desktop with no bar at all. MEASURED, before this door existed: the session's Dock became the active application on its first click and Workspace's menu bar disappeared.
**IT IS ABOUT THE KEYBOARD AND NOT ABOUT THE POINTER.** A non-activatable window still receives every pointer event it is under: it can be clicked, dragged from and hovered, and its own controls work. What it never does is BECOME THE APPLICATION IN FRONT — the focus stays exactly where it was, which is what makes a click on a tile able to move the focus to somebody else without a storm of intermediate activations.
**IT IS ALSO NOT A POLICY ABOUT LEVELS.** The window server does not decide that "dock-level windows do not activate": a panel or a palette at any level may ask for the same thing, and an application window that wants the ordinary behaviour says nothing at all. Default is activatable.

arg.name: activatable
arg.summary: zero: clicking this window never takes the keyboard

request.name: take_focus

description.summary: make this window key, and take the keyboard with it

request.description:
**`-makeKeyWindow`, SAID TO THE SERVER.** Focus in this server is the seat's: the click path gives it, and a shell's `activate_window` gives it. Neither is available to an application making one of its OWN windows key — which is what `-[NSWindow makeKeyAndOrderFront:]` and a `showWindow:` do, and what an application that just opened a window (a Dock's reopen, a File > New) is doing. Without this the window came forward and the KEYBOARD STAYED WHERE IT WAS: MEASURED, a reopened Workspace window was frontmost in the list and typing went to the desktop behind it.
It does not restack: `raise` is the other half and a caller orders the window itself. A window that has said `set_activatable 0` is refused here like everywhere else, because the seat checks once for all doors.

event.name: reopen

description.summary: the shell asked this application to show a window again

event.description:
**THE APPLICATION'S ANSWER IS THE POINT.** A Dock tile was clicked and this application was running without a window a person could work in — nothing above the furniture levels, which is Workspace whenever its desktop is on the screen and no file window is. The application decides what that click means: it may open a window, raise one it had hidden, or do nothing at all, and the AppKit puts the question to its delegate as `-applicationShouldHandleReopen:hasVisibleWindows:`.
THIS WINDOW IS NOT NAMED BY THE EVENT, because the answer need not be this window — it is the address the question arrived at, nothing more.

event.name: dock_menu_requested

description.summary: a shell is asking this application for its dock menu

event.description:
**THE APPLICATION'S ANSWER IS `set_dock_menu`, AND IT IS ASKED RATHER THAN CACHED.** A dock menu is a picture of what the application can do at this moment, so the only moment it may be built is the moment it is about to be shown. The AppKit puts the question to its delegate as `-applicationDockMenu:` — Apple's own door, declared in this tree long before there was a Dock to ask it — and the answer goes straight back.
**AN APPLICATION MUST ANSWER, EVEN WITH NOTHING TO SAY**, because the Dock is holding a menu open for it: `set_dock_menu` with an empty string is the answer "no items of my own", and it costs one request. A client that never answers leaves the Dock to its timeout, which is the only thing a shell can do about an application that has stopped reading its own events.

request.name: set_dock_menu

description.summary: the answer to `dock_menu_requested`

request.description:
The menu, in the application's own format (see `agora_dock_menu.menu`), or an empty string for "none". The server hands it to every client still waiting on this window and forgets it: a dock menu is not part of a window's state, it is the answer to a question, and there is nothing to keep.
An answer nobody asked for is ignored rather than refused — the ask it belonged to may have timed out or the Dock may have gone away, and neither is the application's fault.

request.name: set_badge

description.summary: the label this application's Dock tile shows

request.description:
**A BADGE IS THE APPLICATION'S OWN ANSWER, PUSHED RATHER THAN ASKED FOR.** The Dock's tile for an application shows a short label — an unread count, a state — and only the application knows when it changes. So the application sends it here, the server keeps it on the window (the only place this protocol keeps application state), and `agora_window_list.window` carries it on the snapshot the Dock already takes.
AN EMPTY STRING CLEARS THE BADGE, which is also what an application that never sets one reports: the ordinary case, and not a failure. A badge set before the application has a window has nowhere to live; the AppKit sends it again on `-[NSDockTile display]`, which is what that door is for.

event.name: dock_menu_action

description.summary: the person chose an item of the menu this application published

event.description: It carries the item's id and nothing else, because the application is the only side that can turn an id back into an object and only it knows what choosing one means. The AppKit finds the `NSMenuItem` in the menu it published and sends its action, which is exactly what its own tracking loop would have done.

request.name: set_buffer_scale_fixed

description.summary: the buffer is this many device pixels per logical point

request.description:
**THE FRACTIONAL HALF OF `wl_surface.set_buffer_scale`, WHICH THE PROTOCOL CANNOT EXPRESS.** A 2x client says "my buffer is twice the surface" with an integer; a resolution-independent client says 1.333 or 0.805 and wants the compositor to place those pixels 1:1 rather than multiply and resample. Sent before the commit that attaches the buffer it describes, exactly like `wl_surface.set_buffer_scale`, and it replaces that integer for this surface while it is set.
The scale MUST be the `agora_output.preferred_scale` the client heard (or a positive fraction of its own choosing for a deliberately scaled surface), and the buffer MUST be `round(frame * scale)` device pixels. The compositor trusts that pair: it places the buffer at its own pixel size, positions it at `round(frame_origin * output_scale)`, and treats the window's frame as the logical size. A client that declares a fraction and attaches a buffer of another size gets a 1:1 placement of the wrong pixels, which is the same class of mistake as `set_buffer_scale` with a buffer that does not match — the protocol has never been able to check a buffer's honesty, and this request does not pretend to.

request.name: set_sheet_parent

description.summary: this window hangs from that window's title bar

request.description:
**A SHEET IS THE FIRST THING ON THIS DESKTOP THAT IS TWO WINDOWS AT ONCE, AND THE SERVER HAS TO BE TOLD.** On the Mac a sheet is a window the application made and the application places — `NSAlert`, `NSSavePanel`, `NSPrintPanel` and every "are you sure?" is an ordinary `NSWindow` with a frame of its own, and `agora_window.set_frame` already moved it. What the server cannot work out for itself is that the two frames belong to each other, and there are two consequences it draws from that:
**1. THE TOP CORNERS ARE THE PARENT'S.** A window's shape here is a rounded rectangle cut by the compositor (a client is opaque on the wire and cannot round its own corners), and a sheet's top edge is not its own edge — it is somebody else's title bar, the seam the sheet slides out of. So its TOP two corners are square, exactly as `agora_output`'s bar gives a menu hanging from the menu bar square top corners, and its bottom two stay round, which is the shape a sheet has. WITHOUT THIS THE NOTCHES SHOW: two six-point bites out of the seam, with the parent's own content behind them. The same seam is why a sheet's SHADOW stops there — above `seam`'s rows and no higher — because a shadow painted onto a title bar is a dark band under a bar that is supposed to be a seam rather than a ledge.
**2. THE SHEET IS EXACTLY ONE LAYER ABOVE ITS PARENT, AND NOTHING CAN BE STACKED BETWEEN THEM.** A click on the parent's title bar, a Dock's `activate_window`, the application's own `-orderFront:` on either the sheet or the parent, or a third window raised in between — every one of those reorders the server's stack, and a sheet left anywhere but immediately in front of its parent is a sheet that can go behind it, or that a neighbour can be interleaved with. So the pair has ONE place in the order, and it is derived rather than maintained: a sheet whose parent is on the screen has no place of its own, is drawn the instant its parent has been, and is hit-tested immediately in front of it. **That also means a sheet's LEVEL IS NOT USED while it is a sheet** — an `NSAlert`'s panel is at `NSModalPanelWindowLevel` and the document it asks about is at 0, and the pair is drawn at the document's place, which is what keeps the alert under the menu bar rather than above it. Raising a sheet raises its family: a sheet is never in front of its parent *and* behind nothing, that being a state the glass cannot show.
**IT PLACES NOTHING AND IT SIZES NOTHING.** Where the sheet hangs and how big it is are the application's, as every frame here is; the AppKit puts the sheet's top edge at its parent's content top and re-pins it when the parent moves. A server that computed the placement would be the second opinion the first paragraph of this protocol is about.
**`parent` IS THE SHEET'S OWN PARENT AND NOT AN ID**, because both windows are the calling client's: a window object belongs to the client that made it, so a client can only ever name a window of its own. That also means the server keeps a POINTER to the parent's surface, and it clears it when the parent goes away — a parent destroyed first leaves the sheet an ordinary window rather than a dangling link.
**NULL DETACHES**, which is what ending a sheet sends. One parent per window: asking again replaces the first, and a sheet that names a window which is itself a sheet is an ordinary window hanging from a title bar it does not have — the server does not police it, because the AppKit already refuses a second sheet on one window and a server that re-derived that rule would be the second copy of it.
**`seam` IS HOW MUCH OF THIS WINDOW'S TOP EDGE IS NOT ITS OWN.** A sheet is placed with its top edge a little way INSIDE the parent's title bar rather than flush with its bottom, which is what makes it read as coming out from under the bar: the client paints that strip in the bar's own colour, so the overlap is invisible, and it is robust where a flush placement is not — two frames rounded independently at a fractional scale can leave one device row of the bar's line showing across the top of the sheet. `seam` names that strip, in logical points, and the server's one use for it is the shadow: a shadow may not be painted on the rows the sheet is tucked into, because those rows belong to the title bar. Zero is the ordinary answer for a client that places its sheet flush.

arg.name: parent
arg.summary: the window this one hangs from, or null to detach

arg.name: seam
arg.summary: points of this window's top edge tucked into the parent's title bar; nothing casts a shadow there

request.name: set_cursor

description.summary: the pointer's shape while it is over this window

request.description:
**THE POINTER IS THE COMPOSITOR'S AND ITS SHAPE IS THE WINDOW'S, WHICH IS WHY THIS CROSSES AT ALL.** Until this request existed the compositor drew its theme's arrow and nothing could say otherwise: an application knew its pointer should be an I-beam over text or a hand over a link, resolved that from its own view tree, installed the right `NSCursor` with `-set` — and the answer died in the AppKit, because there was no wire. `wl_pointer.set_cursor` is the protocol's other answer and it is a different one: that carries a SURFACE of the client's own pixels, and it makes every application ship an arrow, an I-beam and a resize cursor for itself.
**A NAME, RESOLVED BY THE COMPOSITOR AGAINST ITS OWN THEME.** The theme is the desktop's design and its cursors are installed already (`aws_cursor_theme_frames`), so what crosses is an Xcursor name — `left_ptr`, `text`, `pointer`, `crosshair`, `not-allowed`, `nwse-resize`, and so on — and the compositor draws the variant its output's scale asks for. That is also what makes this work at a fractional scale: the client names a shape, the server picks the artwork.
**THE WINDOW, NOT THE SEAT.** The shape follows what the pointer is OVER, so two windows of one application can ask for two different pointers and the compositor shows the one belonging to the window the pointer is in. A per-seat request would have made that impossible for the reason the AppKit's own model resolves per window: the answer is a function of the view under the pointer, and a seat has no views.
**AN EMPTY STRING IS THE DEFAULT** (`left_ptr`), which is what a window says when its views have no opinion. **`none` IS A SHAPE AND NOT AN EMPTY NAME**: it means the pointer is not drawn at all, and it is the answer for a video player or a page that draws its own pointer — a fallback to the arrow there would put our pointer on top of theirs. A name the theme does not have falls back to the default, and the compositor says so once, when it changes, rather than on every motion.
**IT IS SENT WHEN THE SHAPE CHANGES, NOT WHEN THE POINTER MOVES.** A motion is sixty events a second; a request per motion would be that many round trips to say the same word. The client is expected to remember what it last said, as the AppKit does (`-cg_applyCursor:`), and a compositor that receives the same name again has nothing to do with it.

arg.name: name
arg.summary: an Xcursor name; empty for the default, `none` to draw nothing
